EarthProsp Atlas

Mineral prospectivity for every land cell on Earth, predicted from AlphaEarth Foundations satellite embeddings (2024). Shown here at H3 resolution 4 (~1,770 km² per hexagon), averaged from 4,489,547 resolution-6 cells.

Cell split

Hover or tap the map to see the predicted split for that hexagon.

What the colour means

With “Any commodity” selected, colour is the prospectivity score: the model’s ranking of how likely a hexagon is to host a deposit of any of the 15 classes. Choosing a commodity colours by that class’s share of the split, P(deposit) × P(class | deposit). Scales stretch to the 99th percentile of each view. Scores rank cells; they are not calibrated probabilities.

How well it works

Scored on whole ~600,000 km² blocks it never saw in training, the top 20% of land by score holds 61% of the held-out deposit cells outside the US and 56% of world-class deposits. Measuring distance to known deposits instead catches 43% and 40%. With an entire continent hidden during training, that continent’s top 20% still holds 60% (Africa), 54% (Australia) and 40% (South America) of its world-class deposits. The commodity split only beats a global-average mix within about 500 km of known deposits, so it fades toward that average further out.

Where not to trust it

AlphaEarth sees the surface. Under glacial cover, rainforest, deep soil and young sediment the map is extrapolation. Training labels are densest in the US, part of the signal reflects visible mining disturbance, and the model has no geophysics yet.
